actions.body: Our inquiry into whether an intelligent system can identify and correct its own foundational assumptions has synthesized key insights from metareasoning-partitioning and neuro-symbolic frameworks. Metareasoning-partition models indicate that rational agents must carefully balance resources between planning and execution [source-336dbab760194b56]. While these models allow agents to optimize for efficiency, they presuppose a goal-directed structure that the agent itself does not define. Separately, neuro-symbolic approaches provide a mechanism for error detection and correction in neural models [source-f0124fd3eddc466d]. These systems can identify deviations from expected behavior in novel environments, effectively 'correcting' the model. However, identifying an assumption as 'inadequate' requires an external or higher-order framework that the agent may not inherently possess. We find that current technology can support error correction and adaptive resource allocation, but the jump to autonomous, foundational re-evaluation of its own axiomatic structure remains an unreached milestone. Summary: We have evaluated how intelligent systems manage their own reasoning processes. We found that while systems can learn to optimize resource use and detect errors in their operations, they currently lack the capability to independently challenge their own fundamental assumptions or axiomatic goals without external guidance.
actions.lede: Can a system truly 'know' its own foundations? Research into metareasoning and error correction suggests we are building the tools for self-critique, but foundations remain elusive.
